Plain-English Guide (2026)", "metaDescription": "A no-code app builder lets you build apps by dragging and configuring, not typing code. Learn how the category works, real examples, and how AI-chat tools like Kodely differ.", "targetKeyword": "what is a no-code app builder", "category": "Glossary", "bodyHtml": "

A no-code app builder is software that lets you build a working app or website by arranging visual elements and setting configuration options, instead of writing programming code. You drag a button onto a canvas, connect it to an action through a menu, and the tool assembles the underlying logic for you. The whole point is to remove typing code from the process entirely.

That definition matters because the term gets used loosely. Plenty of tools that generate code from a written description also get called "no-code," even though something quite different is happening under the hood. This guide covers what the category actually means, how it works, a few real examples, and where newer AI-chat tools fit in relation to it.

How no-code app builders actually work

Every no-code builder is built around the same core idea: configuration over code. Instead of a text editor and a compiler, you get a visual canvas and a set of pre-built blocks. A few patterns show up across almost every tool in the category:

  • Drag-and-drop layout. You place elements — text, images, buttons, forms, lists — directly onto a page or screen and position them visually.
  • Visual logic. Instead of writing an if/else statement, you set up a rule through dropdowns and condition panels: "when this button is clicked, show that screen."
  • Pre-built data structures. Most no-code builders include a built-in database or data layer with a spreadsheet-like interface for defining fields and relationships, no schema code required.
  • Templates and components. Reusable blocks — login forms, product cards, navigation bars — get dropped in and customized through settings panels rather than built from scratch.

The output is usually an app that runs inside the platform itself, or one the platform hosts and serves on your behalf. You are configuring a system the vendor already built, not producing an independent, portable codebase.

Real examples of the category

A few well-known tools illustrate what "no-code" has traditionally meant:

  • Webflow — a visual builder for marketing sites and web pages, where you design directly on a canvas and Webflow handles the underlying HTML and CSS.
  • Bubble — a visual builder for full web applications, including custom logic and a built-in database, aimed at people building product-style apps without writing code.
  • Adalo and Glide — builders focused on mobile-style apps, often built by turning a spreadsheet or visual layout into a functioning app.

These tools differ in scope and audience, but they share the same mechanism: you build by manipulating a visual interface, and the platform translates that into a running app.

Why it matters, and who it's for

No-code app builders exist to lower the barrier between an idea and a working product. They're aimed at people who don't write code — founders, marketers, small business owners, internal ops teams — and who need something functional without hiring a developer or learning a programming language. The tradeoff is that you're working within the vendor's visual system: what you can build is bounded by the components, logic blocks, and integrations that platform provides.

How AI-chat builders like Kodely differ

This is where the terminology gets confusing, and it's worth being precise about it. A no-code builder works through visual configuration — you never see or touch code, because you're arranging pre-built pieces. An AI-chat builder like Kodely works through a written description that produces real code — you type what you want in plain English, and the tool writes actual source files behind the scenes.

Kodely generates a real Vite + React + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS application: genuine .tsx component files, not a visual mockup and not a proprietary internal format. You can open the code view and read the exact files that make up your app. That's a meaningfully different category from dragging elements onto a canvas — it's closer to having a developer type the code for you than to configuring a no-code platform. Some people use "no-code" loosely to describe both, but only one of them is actually visual/drag-and-drop; the other is AI-generated code.

Where Kodely fits today

To be precise about current scope: Kodely is a frontend app builder. Describe a site in chat, and it generates a real React app with a live preview of the compiled result. Publishing puts it live on a free yourname.kodely.site subdomain in one click, and every successful generation creates a checkpoint you can roll back to for free. Further changes happen the same way — describe them in chat, and Kodely edits the real components.

It does not yet generate backends, databases, authentication, or payment systems, and it doesn't support custom domains or code export as a zip file. There's no click-to-edit visual canvas — all editing goes through chat. New accounts start with 750 free credits, no card required, and a build that fails to compile is never charged.

Related terms

  • Low-code — platforms that mix visual building with the option to drop into real code for advanced logic, sitting between no-code and traditional development.
  • AI app builder — a broader term covering any tool that uses AI to generate part or all of an app from a prompt, whether the output is code or a visual configuration.
  • Vibe coding — building software by describing what you want in natural language and letting an AI write the code, rather than typing it yourself.

FAQ

Is Kodely a no-code tool?

Not in the traditional sense. Kodely doesn't use drag-and-drop or visual configuration — you describe your app in chat, and it generates real React code. It's more accurately described as an AI code generator with a conversational interface, which lands in a different category than tools like Webflow or Bubble even though the end result — not writing code yourself — feels similar.

Do I need to know how to code to use a no-code builder?

No. That's the defining feature of the category — you build entirely through a visual interface. The same is true of AI-chat tools like Kodely: you describe what you want, and the code gets written for you.

What's the difference between no-code and AI-generated code?

No-code means the app is assembled from visual, pre-built components with no code involved at any stage. AI-generated code means a real codebase is produced from a natural-language description — the code exists and can be inspected, even though you didn't type it.

Can I see the actual code behind my app in Kodely?

Yes. Kodely includes a code view where you can see and copy the real generated source files. There's no zip export yet, but the files themselves are visible in-app.

Ready to see the difference between configuring an app and describing one? Build free on Kodely and generate a real React app from a plain-English description.
